claims.title: Wheelchair turning circles
claims.explanation: SuRaKu: clear turning diameter at least 1.5 m for a wheelchair, 2.5 m for a powered wheelchair. The sheet draws them at a common scale. Keep the usable envelope clear (editorial application of clear-space guidance); do not infer that every mobility scooter fits this envelope.

references.location: Card 3, PDF p. 5; also card 4 p. 7 and card 7 p. 13

claims.title: Seating and accessible parking
claims.explanation: SuRaKu: wheelchair space ≥0.9 m at a bench end; backs, armrests and varied seat heights. Courtyard accessible bay ≥3.6 × 5 m, gradient ≤2% both directions. Kerbside bays and vehicle transfer/lift access need separate layouts. SuRaKu card 5 recommends resting places on park routes at 50 m intervals at special accessibility level and at most 250 m at basic level.

references.location: Card 5, resting-place spacing on park routes

claims.title: Rescue geometry
claims.explanation: HIKLU: fire engine and aerial appliance route width 3.5 m, clear height 4.2 m. Inner/outer radii: engine 5/10.5 m; aerial 5.5/12.5 m. Aerial set-up width ≥6 m, target 8 m, length 13 m. The vehicle models also specify driving allowance 0.4 m and aerial boom allowance 1.0 m. Our circles do not add these allowances or simulate a manoeuvre. Check loads, slopes, reach, trees, wires and snow against the complete guide.

claims.title: Tree soil volume
claims.explanation: Helsinki’s draft tree-and-tram card gives approximately 25 m³ conventional soil for a large-growing tree and discusses 40–60 m³ structural soil because stone displaces water storage. These are contextual indicative volumes, not a universal minimum. Coordinate roots, utilities and mature crown; grouped trees should have continuous soil.

references.location: Puiden kasvualustan mitoitus; source marked draft

claims.title: Detention example
claims.explanation: Espoo’s Kaavoitus section gives an example zoning provision: 1 m³ per 100 m² impermeable surface, emptying in 12–24 h and controlled overflow. It is not asserted for this site. Example calculation: 600/100 = 6 m³; at assumed 0.20 m effective depth, 6/0.20 = 30 m² idealised plan area. Side slopes, freeboard, ground conditions and actual inflow/outflow are not calculated.

claims.title: Slab and point-block footprints
claims.explanation: TKK drawing: one slab module 22–30 m long and 10–12 m deep, repeated to make longer buildings. The new plan draws two 26 × 11 m modules. The square point-block variant is at most 20 × 20 m, drawn at that size. All building plans on the sheet share a uniform scale; these are historical footprints, not current building rights.

claims.title: Small blocks and row houses
claims.explanation: TKK: small-apartment repeated module 8–10 m in each direction; row dwelling 4–8 m wide, building depth 8–11 m and garden depth approximately 5–15 m. The new plans draw four 9 × 9 m small-block modules and four 6 × 9.5 m row dwellings with 10 m gardens. The repeated module width is not the entire building length.

claims.title: Detached-house footprint
claims.explanation: TKK one-storey example: approximately 15 × 10 m house, plot approximately 500–1,000 m². The new plan uses a 25 × 30 m = 750 m² example plot. Plot shape and house position are editorial; the old boundary-setback dimension is not adopted as a current rule.

claims.title: Historic density examples and the denominator
claims.explanation: TKK gives e = total floor area / selected land area. Its table, attributed to Asuntoalueen mitoitus – tunnuslukuja, compiled by Tarja Behnke, lists detached: district .04–.10, block .10–.15, plot .05–.15, about 30 residents/ha; linked low-rise: about .20, .25–.35, about .35, about 50; row houses: .30, .35–.40, about .40, about 75; apartments up to 7 storeys: .40, average .65, about .70, about 100. These are historical examples, not a population formula. Land boundaries and occupancy must be stated.

claims.title: Historic recreation-area hierarchy
claims.explanation: TKK: plot play/stay within 50 m, 10 m² organised play per 100 m² residential floor area, minimum 100 m² and one play area per 3,000 floor-m². Neighbourhood park within 150 m, 25 m² per 100 residential floor-m², minimum 3,500–4,000 m². The following 1,500–2,000 m² sub-allocation has no stated purpose in the source and is omitted. District recreation within 500 m, minimum 10 ha including 0.6–1.2 ha play park; sizing depends on building density and nature. Recreation route length 3–10 km. This is the historical provision hierarchy, not modern RAMS maintenance classification. Bars compare distances, not network catchment areas.

claims.title: Public services: three different population measures
claims.explanation: Library: the 2010 ministry recommendation is about 100 m² useful floor area per 1,000 residents, with small municipalities often needing more per capita. The 10 × 10 m square visualises area only. Seinäjoki’s 2017 plan says population growth beyond 2,000 would bring a primary school and daycare; nearby schools were full. This is additional population and a local capacity trigger. Helsinki’s 2020 proposal assigns roughly 20,000 residents to an additional central-city health-station unit. It is a case population responsibility, not a minimum viable settlement. No universal service threshold is inferred; age structure, current capacity and catchment remain site inputs. TKK’s public-services section was unfinished; these are new sources.

claims.title: Footway, clear widths and route gradients
claims.explanation: Espoo: 2.5 m basic footway. SuRaKu card 1: 1.5 m clear passage, 1.8 m wheelchair passing and 2.3 m machine maintenance. Route crossfall special/basic ≤2%/3%; longitudinal gradient ≤5%/8%. Ramps have separate guidance. Selectable width sections share one fixed scale; pavement thickness is illustrative. Light-grey filled front-elevation people are drawn exactly 1.75 m tall. Height and posture are declared illustration assumptions, not population percentiles. A person silhouette is not the accessible clear-space envelope. Four presets display 2.5, 1.5, 1.8 and 2.3 m at one fixed scale, shared with the cycling-width drawings.

references.location: Printed p. 8, table 1: pedestrian design width .6 m

claims.title: Bicycle envelope and handling space
claims.explanation: Helsinki typical cycle envelope is 0.6 m wide, 2 m long, 1.2 m high. Its rough one-row allowance is number of cycles × (0.6 m × 4 m), including handling space. Our plan shows five envelopes plus the remaining 2 m handling strip, not a specified rack design. Some racks need more length; special/cargo cycles require separate assessment. Espoo 811A keeps cycle/scooter parking out of the 5 m before specified crossings.

claims.title: Ramp width, gradient and landings
claims.explanation: SuRaKu: ramp minimum width 0.9 m, recommended minimum 1.2 m; recommended gradient ≤5%, maximum 8%. On long ramps steeper than 5%, straight intermediate landings at least 2 m every 6 m. The drawing is an illustrative 0.30 m rise at 5%: horizontal run = 0.30 / .05 = 6 m, followed by a 2 m landing. Both axes use the same scale. A 2 m landing drawn here does not imply that this particular short 5% ramp triggers the long-ramp rule. The landing includes a 1.75 m illustrative person at the same metric scale; body height/posture are drawing assumptions.

claims.title: Tram line corridors and lateral clearances
claims.explanation: Espoo 2010 reserves at least 8 m for light rail, with stops separate. Helsinki’s draft street-space card gives at least 6 m for a line section. These are different source contexts. Regional guide: track centres on straight slab track at least 3 m; ballasted track minimum 3.1 m (3 m is approval-only). Normal separation from ATU edge to walking/cycling is 0.80 m at ≤40 km/h, 1.15 m at 50 km/h and 1.50 m above 50 km/h. Normal values are the general-planning starting point. Curves, poles, evacuation and crossings are additional design checks. Uncanted curve radii from the regional geometry table at 0.65 m/s² lateral acceleration: 48 m at 20 km/h, 107 m at 30 km/h, 190 m at 40 km/h. Transitions and clearance widening remain additional.

references.location: General principles and table 1, normal clearance column
§3.1.1 track centres and §3.1.2 table 2, zero cant row

claims.title: Tram stop cross-section
claims.explanation: Regional tram guide: normal side-platform width 3.5 m; straight dedicated double-track width between platforms 5.5 m. The derived two-sided example totals 12.5 m before outer paths/buffers; its longitudinal diagram extent is arbitrary. Clear passage normal ≥1.8 m, minimum 1.5 m; island platform minimum 5 m. Passenger-space guide: 1 m²/person, minimum .75 m²/person, dimensioned using peak-period boarding demand. These are not automatically cumulative independent strips; shelter, waiting and circulation must fit the platform. Curves and mixed-traffic stops differ.

claims.title: Tram stop length and levels
claims.explanation: Regional guide: light-rail flat service area normally 45 m, 35 m by project agreement; Helsinki city-tram-only stop 30 m for one or 61 m for two. Add access ramps and crossing waiting areas. Ramp maximum 5%; platform longitudinal gradient normally ≤2%, crossfall 1–2%. Height above rail generally .30 m, Helsinki normally .27 m; select the vehicle/network context. The example assumes .30 m rise from adjacent level: .30/.05 = 6 m ramp at each end, hence 45 + 6 + 6 = 57 m before crossing waiting areas. The source’s approximate 5–5.5 m ramps depend on actual road/platform levels; the drawing uses its explicit assumption, not that approximate range. The stop plan includes two nominal 34 × 2.4 m tram-body silhouettes based on the regional guide’s five-part Artic XL table. Bodies and stop geometry share a scale. Joint/window details are illustrative; these are not the ATU clearance envelopes.

references.location: §2.4 platform lengths, ramps, heights and slopes
Table 1, Artic XL five-part nominal length/width

claims.title: Historical car/van turning band
claims.explanation: TKK car/van diagram has 3 m inner and 6.5 m outer radius. The new graphic is an exact quarter annulus with a direction arrow and centre/radius lines. No wheelbase, body or steering trajectory is given in the source; the band therefore is not represented as a computed swept path. W4 lists servicing and excludes long-term private car parking. A separate original plan silhouette uses the 5.0 × 1.8 m reference car body listed in the Helsinki development drawing. It shares the radius-band scale, but is not placed on a simulated path. Mirrors, wheelbase and body detailing are not design geometry. Additional presets show one 3 m lane or two 3 m lanes, derived total 6 m, using the lower end of Espoo’s 3–3.25 m local-collector range. Plan length 18 m is illustrative. One/two-lane plans share a scale; kerbs, separation, parking and other modes are additional.

references.location: Reference vehicle data on the parking swept-path drawing

claims.title: Historical bus turn and Espoo stop lengths
claims.explanation: TKK bus turn uses inner radius 8.1 m and outer radius 15.2 m, redrawn as a quarter-annulus reference. Espoo local-collector lanes are 3–3.25 m, minimum 3.25 m where buses govern. Espoo stop 031D uses a 15 m design bus, with 16 m one-bus and 32 m two-bus stop service lengths; approaches/crossings need the full drawing. The historic band and modern stop drawing are separate contexts. A separate original bus silhouette uses the Espoo 15 m design length and 2.6 m body width (Appendix B). It shares the radius-band scale. Mirrors are omitted; detailing is schematic. It does not establish that this vehicle follows the historical TKK band. Additional presets show one 3.25 m bus-governed lane or two such lanes, derived total 6.5 m, at one fixed scale. Plan length 18 m is illustrative; other street components remain additional.

references.location: Stop lengths and separate approach requirements
Appendix B p. 3, vehicle body widths; main guide p. 16 design-bus length

claims.title: Planting-strip widths and winter coordination
claims.explanation: Espoo 2010 planting widths: trees ≥3 m, main streets ≥3.5 m, low shrubs ≥2.5 m, lawn/ground cover ≥2 m. Bar thicknesses are illustrative. Width does not determine adequate soil volume. Coordination of roots/utilities, canopy/wires, snow/salt and rescue access is an editorial synthesis of the guides, not a new universal snow-storage dimension.

claims.title: Street width-to-height ratio
claims.explanation: W5 explicitly asks for sections showing surrounding urban structure and W/H ratio. The helper defines the measured façade-to-façade W and stated reference H. Three geometric examples use H=12 m and W=12, 24, 36 m, giving W/H=1, 2, 3 at one graphic scale. Building depth is arbitrary. No optimal ratio or storey-height assumption is claimed. Unequal sides need both heights identified.

claims.title: Equal floor-area ratio, different massing
claims.explanation: Geometric illustration: each plot is 32 × 32 = 1,024 m². Coverage 50%, 25%, 12.5% with 2, 4, 8 identical floor plates gives 1,024 m² floor area and e=1 for each. These are editorial configurations, not building rights or resident-density conversions. Different forms can have the same area ratio.

claims.title: Outdoor stair reference
claims.explanation: SuRaKu 2008 card 3 gives minimum stair width 1.2 m, rise 0.12 m and recommended outdoor relationship 2 × rise + tread = .66 m. Hence the example tread is .42 m; the profile uses equal scales and identical steps. Covered/heated stairs use .63 m instead. Rest landing recommended every 10–15 steps; edge contrast strip 30–40 mm. This dated reference is not a complete current building-regulation or guard/handrail specification.

claims.title: CAD units, geometry and limits
claims.explanation: Canonical coordinates are metres. DXF factor / INSUNITS: m=1/6; mm=1,000/4; international ft=(1/.3048)/2. R2000 entities are rounded to four selected-unit decimals. SVG uses the selected drawing units in its viewBox; browser pixels are not print scale. Seven template sets: historical building representatives; accessible clear space; historic car/bus inner/outer circles and quarter arcs; rescue circles and set-up; tram 45 m platforms and 5.5 m track zone; independent street strips; a dated eight-bay parking module. Actual example values, arbitrary lengths, extra allowances and evidence are labelled. No editable calculators or live width-budget export remain.

claims.title: Rain gardens and vegetated swales
claims.explanation: Rain gardens combine temporary ponding, filtration, vegetation and, where conditions allow, infiltration. Swales convey water slowly; checks can increase storage. Drains and overflow provide discharge routes. The diagrams are conceptual: no filter depth, ponding depth or infiltration rate is specified. Soil, groundwater, contamination and maintenance need project-specific checks. These are design considerations, not additional course deliverables.

claims.title: Dry basins, permanent ponds and wetlands
claims.explanation: Helsinki describes basins that empty between rains and basins with permanent water. Wetlands use shallow water and varied planted levels, typically tens of centimetres deep. Its indicative natural basin/wetland slopes are 1 vertical to 4–5 horizontal. The water-storage sections are conceptual. A separate dimensioned slope triangle shows 1 m vertical / 4 m horizontal = 25%; 1:5 means 20%. Live detention is the available volume above normal water level; full permanent water volume cannot be counted as empty storage. Outlet, overflow, banks and access must be included in the layout.

claims.title: Green roofs, permeable paving, reuse and treatment chains
claims.explanation: HSY lists green roofs, rain gardens and rainwater collection/reuse as runoff-reduction options, and surface or underground storage for gradual release. Permeable-pavement aggregate stores water in its voids; infiltration/drainage and clogging maintenance must be checked, including winter conditions. The roof and paving sections are conceptual, with no prescribed thickness or capacity. The matrix identifies design inputs rather than numerical requirements; roof wet load and storage availability require structural/hydrological design. A combined chain can reduce runoff, treat it, store it and discharge through controlled overflow.

references.location: Executive summary and winter maintenance chapters
Opening treatment-chain principles and permeable surfaces

claims.title: Independent CAD width strips
claims.explanation: Espoo 2010 widths: basic footway 2.5 m, one-way cycle lane 1.75 m, tree strip 3 m, bus-governed local-collector lane 3.25 m and light-rail reservation 8 m. Each strip is arbitrarily 20 m long and drawn separately. Their combination is not a prescribed section; add separation, kerbs, snow, drainage, utilities and stops as applicable.

claims.title: Cycling layout options at a fixed graphic scale
claims.explanation: Espoo 2010: one-way cycle lane 1.75 m, shared walk/cycle path 3–4 m, separated walk/cycle total 4 m (main route at least 4.5 m), parking-side buffer at least .75 m. Helsinki May 2014, printed p. 19: two-way track at footway level has effective width 2.5–4 m on main routes depending on volumes; quality corridors target at least 3.5 m. Other routes have a separate 2.2–2.5 m range. Our options draw 2.5 m and 3.5 m, not the full range. Walking and the road-side separation strip are additional; Helsinki specifies a road-side strip of at least 1 m, enlarged for snow. Different facility types and editions are not interchangeable. All five width options retain the same scale; figures do not imply crowd or traffic capacity. The light-grey rider is 1.65 m high including the illustrated helmet, with .60 m handlebars; height/posture are declared assumptions. A separate dashed .75 m design-user width comes from Helsinki 2014 table 1. Rider, envelope, lane and walking-panel figures use one uniform metric scale. Body width does not replace lateral movement clearance. Dot/cross symbols indicate towards/away in the cycle-only sections; rider posture is schematic.

references.location: Printed p. 19, two-way track at footway level

claims.title: Crossing refuge and its place in the street section
claims.explanation: Espoo 2010 §6 says a crossing-refuge island is at least 2.5 m wide, likewise a median crossed by a walking/cycling route. In this plan that dimension is measured along the pedestrian crossing. Two illustrative 3 m local-collector lanes plus the 2.5 m refuge give an 8.5 m span before outer kerbs/routes. The 4 m crossing-opening width, 8 m island length and schematic stripe dimensions are declared illustration assumptions, not dimensions taken from the source. The plan does not prescribe a full junction, kerb or tactile-warning detail. Coordination of kerb direction cues, drainage and the continuing clear route follows SuRaKu card 1. The drawing adds no course deliverable.

references.location: Printed p. 19, §6: crossing islands and medians; p. 16 for local-collector lane range
Card 1, crossing arrangements, direction cues and clear routes

claims.title: Walking route versus straight-line proximity
claims.explanation: This is an explicitly invented geometric example, not a catchment recommendation. The entrance and destination share a y-coordinate and are 300 m apart. The only drawn connection follows 100 m to a bridge, 300 m across, then 100 m back: 500 m, an additional 200 m. Both axes use the same scale. No walking speed, service viability threshold, crossing delay or site condition is inferred. River/bridge symbols and the network are illustrative. The example explains why the historical TKK proximity figures on the other sheet do not alone demonstrate an actual usable walking catchment. The new prompts to trace connections and check access conditions are assistant-drafted design reasoning consistent with W4 integration, not additional assignments.

references.location: Historical green-area distance examples; no new distance threshold inferred
Selected source paragraphs 19, 40 and 50: spatial elements, variation along the street and integration

claims.title: Continuous horizontal and vertical pedestrian clearance
claims.explanation: SuRaKu 2008 card 1 gives unobstructed route width at least 1.5 m, two-wheelchair passing width at least 1.8 m and clear pedestrian height at least 2.2 m. Beneath a building or part of a building it recommends at least 3 m. These are dated outdoor pedestrian guidance, not cycle/tram/vehicle clearances or a statement of current building regulations. The new plan example assumes 2.5 m total pavement width and 1.1 m encroachment, leaving 1.4 m, below the cited 1.5 m unobstructed width. The 12 m plan length and obstacle length 1.4 m are illustrative. The separate elevation uses uniform metric scale, 1.75 m illustrative people and the cited 2.2/3 m heights; 3 m horizontal envelope widths are illustrative. Seasonal snow, furniture and other obstacles are coordination considerations, not assigned capacities or new course obligations.

references.location: Card 1: Kulkuväylät ja -pinnat, route widths and free height
Printed p. 11, §3.5 accessibility and winter snow-space provision

claims.title: Parking-bay and aisle dimensions
claims.explanation: The 90° reference layout uses a 2.5 × 5 m interior bay and a 7 m two-way manoeuvring aisle. These values appear in TKK 2007 and Salo’s 2016 park-and-ride report; they are dated layout examples, not a claim that every present-day parking facility uses the same dimensions. TKK gives at least 2.75 m for an end bay. The repeating interior module does not include that end condition. Accessible parking is a separate layout: SuRaKu’s courtyard reference is at least 3.6 × 5 m, with at most 2% gradient in both directions; transfer, lift access and street-side layouts need their own checks. Vehicle bodies, if shown, use the separately cited reference silhouette dimensions and do not prove manoeuvrability.

references.location: Reference car body: 5 × 1.8 m; details schematic

claims.title: Bay area versus a repeating parking module
claims.explanation: Geometric example derived from 2.5 m bay width, 5 m depth and a 7 m shared aisle: one bay is 12.5 m². Two facing bays plus their aisle strip occupy 2.5 × (5 + 7 + 5) = 42.5 m², or 21.25 m² per space. The aisle contributes 8.75 m² per space. Salo’s example gives 425 m² for 20 spaces using the same geometry. This is a repeating interior parking-and-aisle module, not the gross area of a complete site or building. Add wider end bays, entrances, pedestrian and accessible routes, landscape, drainage and snow storage; garages also need structures and ramps. No universal gross m²/space allowance is asserted.

references.location: Printed p. 16: 20-space / 425 m² example and figure 11

claims.title: Dated municipal residential parking minima
claims.explanation: These are municipal apartment-building examples, not Finnish national ratios. Helsinki’s 9 Dec 2025 guidance gives at least one space per 250, 230 or 200 m² of statutory floor area in mapped zones 2, 3 or 4. In mapped general-plan centres C1/C2/C3, add 30 m² to the denominator. The zone map is essential; the zones are not simple station-distance rings. Fractions round upward. The city says a guidance minimum need not meet market demand. Espoo’s 2025 guide gives central-core apartment minima of one space per 130, 110 or 95 floor-m² for area classes I, II or III, typically 0–300 m from the station/core. Every apartment case also requires at least 0.5 space per dwelling; satisfy both constraints. At least 5% of the required spaces are visitor spaces. The source table has different values farther from the core, and separate conditional reductions. Check the applicable detailed plan, zone and project conditions; these reference examples do not replace them. They do not override the W4 exclusion of long-term private-car parking.
